section.title: Nicodemus and the New Birth
section.sectionRationale: A leading Pharisee comes to Jesus by night, and Jesus meets his cautious admiration with a demand that cannot be met by effort: you must be born again. The conversation opens out into the Gospel's most famous words, that God so loved the world He gave His only Son. The chapter closes with John the Baptist's last, self-effacing testimony, He must increase, I must decrease.
section.thesis: Entry into the kingdom of God is not by human descent, effort, or learning but by a birth from above, worked by the Spirit, and grounded in the Son of Man lifted up like the serpent in the wilderness, so that everyone who believes in the Son whom God gave in love will not perish but have eternal life.
section.frameNote: Four movements: Nicodemus and the necessity of the new birth from above; the earthly and heavenly witness and the Son of Man lifted up; God's love in giving His Son and the verdict of light and darkness; and John the Baptist's final testimony that Christ must increase.

units.label: You must be born again
units.note: the new birth by the Spirit

verses.text: Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a leader of the Jews.
He came to Jesus at night and said, “Rabbi, we know that You are a teacher who has come from God. For no one could perform the signs You are doing if God were not with him.”
Jesus replied, “Truly, truly, I tell you, no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is {{anothen|born again}}.”
“How can a man be born when he is old?” Nicodemus asked. “Can he enter his mother’s womb a second time to be born?”
Jesus answered, “Truly, truly, I tell you, no one can enter the kingdom of God unless he is born of water and the {{pneuma|Spirit}}.
Flesh is born of flesh, but spirit is born of the Spirit.
Do not be amazed that I said, ‘You must be born again.’
The wind blows where it wishes. You hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it is going. So it is with everyone born of the Spirit.”

units.label: Earthly and heavenly things
units.note: the Son of Man must be lifted up

verses.text: “How can this be?” Nicodemus asked.
“You are Israel’s teacher,” said Jesus, “and you do not understand these things?
Truly, truly, I tell you, we speak of what we know, and we testify to what we have seen, and yet you people do not accept our testimony.
If I have told you about earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you about heavenly things?
No one has ascended into heaven except the One who descended from heaven, the Son of Man.
Just as Moses {{hupsoo|lifted up}} the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up,
that everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life.

units.label: God so loved the world
units.note: the verdict of light and darkness

verses.text: For God so {{agapao|loved}} the world that He gave His one and only Son, that everyone who believes in Him shall not perish but have {{zoe|eternal life}}.
For God did not send His Son into the world to condemn the world, but to save the world through Him.
Whoever believes in Him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe has already been condemned, because he has not believed in the name of God’s one and only Son.
And this is the {{krisis|verdict}}: The Light has come into the world, but men loved the darkness rather than the Light because their deeds were evil.
Everyone who does evil hates the Light, and does not come into the Light for fear that his deeds will be exposed.
But whoever practices the truth comes into the Light, so that it may be seen clearly that what he has done has been accomplished in God.”
After this, Jesus and His disciples went into the Judean countryside, where He spent some time with them and baptized.
Now John was also baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because the water was plentiful there, and people kept coming to be baptized.
(For John had not yet been thrown into prison.)
Then a dispute arose between John’s disciples and a certain Jew over the issue of ceremonial washing.
So John’s disciples came to him and said, “Look, Rabbi, the One who was with you beyond the Jordan, the One you testified about, He is baptizing, and everyone is going to Him.”
John replied, “A man can receive only what is given him from heaven.
You yourselves can testify that I said, ‘I am not the Christ, but am sent ahead of Him.’
The bride belongs to the bridegroom. The friend of the bridegroom stands and listens for him, and is overjoyed to hear the bridegroom’s voice. That joy is mine, and it is now complete.
He must increase; I must decrease.
The One who comes from above is above all. The one who is from the earth belongs to the earth and speaks as one from the earth. The One who comes from heaven is above all.
He testifies to what He has seen and heard, yet no one accepts His testimony.
Whoever accepts His testimony has certified that God is truthful.
For the One whom God has sent speaks the words of God, for God gives the Spirit without limit.
The Father loves the Son and has placed all things in His hands.
Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life. Whoever rejects the Son will not see life. Instead, the wrath of God remains on him.”

anothen.gloss: Again, anew, or from above. The word carries both senses at once, and the double meaning drives the conversation: Nicodemus hears born again and thinks of a second physical birth, but Jesus means born from above, a birth that only God can give. The new birth is not self-improvement but a fresh origin from heaven.

pneuma.gloss: Spirit, wind, or breath, the same word for all three. Jesus exploits the overlap: the wind blows where it wishes, unseen and sovereign, and so it is with everyone born of the Spirit. The new birth is the sovereign, mysterious work of God's Spirit, who gives life where and as He wills.

hupsoo.gloss: To lift up, raise high, exalt. In John the word has a deliberate double sense: Jesus will be physically lifted up on the cross and thereby lifted up in glory. As Moses raised the bronze serpent so the bitten might look and live, the Son of Man is lifted up so that all who look to Him in faith may have eternal life.

agapao.gloss: To love, the verb of the noun agape, a love that gives and seeks the good of another. God so loved the world that He gave His Son; this is love defined by costly self-giving, not mere sentiment. The measure of the love is the gift, the one and only Son, and its aim is that believers should not perish but live.

zoe.gloss: Life, specifically eternal life, the life of the age to come and the very life of God. In John eternal life is not only endless duration but a quality of life that begins now in knowing the Father and the Son. It is the gift given to everyone who believes in the Son who was lifted up.

krisis.gloss: Judgment, verdict, decision. The coming of the Light is itself the verdict; people are judged by whether they come to the Light or hide from it. Jesus came not to condemn but to save, yet the response to Him divides humanity, and unbelief is self-condemnation, a preferring of darkness to light.

basic.context: Nicodemus, a respected Pharisee and teacher, comes to Jesus under cover of darkness with a careful compliment. Jesus cuts past it to the heart of the matter: no one can even see God's kingdom unless he is born again, born from above. Nicodemus is baffled, and Jesus explains that this birth is the work of the Spirit, as free and mysterious as the wind. Then comes the heart of the Gospel: God so loved the world that He gave His only Son. The chapter ends with John the Baptist gladly stepping into the background so that Jesus can take center stage.
basic.hermeneutics: The key questions are, how does anyone enter God's kingdom, and what has God done about our need. Jesus answers that entry is by new birth, which we cannot produce; it is God's gift by the Spirit. And the ground of that gift is the Son lifted up on the cross, given out of God's love. Notice the play on words, born again and from above, wind and Spirit, lifted up on a cross and in glory. Faith is looking to the lifted-up Son, as Israel looked to the bronze serpent and lived.
basic.originalLanguages: The dialogue turns on double meanings. Anothen means both again and from above; Jesus means a birth from heaven. Pneuma means both wind and Spirit; the new birth is as sovereign and unseen as the wind. Hupsoo, lifted up, points to both the cross and the exaltation. God's agape love gives the Son so that believers may have zoe, eternal life, and the coming of the Light is itself the krisis, the verdict.
basic.typology: Moses lifting up the bronze serpent so that the dying might look and live is a direct picture of Christ lifted up on the cross, that whoever looks to Him in faith may live. The new birth by water and the Spirit fulfills the prophets' promise of cleansing and a new heart.
basic.christ: Christ is the One who came down from heaven and will be lifted up on the cross. He is the only Son whom God gave in love, the Light that has come into the world, the bridegroom whose joy John shares. To believe in Him is to have eternal life; to reject Him is to remain under wrath.
basic.god: God is love, and His love is not passive; it gives at the highest cost, His one and only Son. He sends the Son not to condemn but to save. He is also holy, so that the rejection of His Son leaves a person under judgment. And He gives the Spirit who alone can bring the new birth.
basic.crossReferences: Numbers 21 tells of the bronze serpent lifted up. Ezekiel 36 promises cleansing with water and a new spirit. 1 Peter 1 speaks of being born again to a living hope. Ephesians 2 describes being made alive by grace.
basic.oneStory: Humanity, fallen and unable to save itself, needs a birth it cannot achieve. In love God gives His Son to be lifted up like the serpent in the wilderness, so that all who look to Him live. The Spirit brings the new birth the prophets promised, and the whole story turns on whether we come to the Light or hide in the dark.

context.literary:
Chapter 3 is built as a pair of conversations that fade into monologue. In verses 1 to 12 Nicodemus speaks three times, each time more briefly and more helplessly: a compliment, a puzzle about a womb, and then the bare question 'How can this be?' After verse 10 he vanishes from the page and Jesus talks on. A similar fading happens in the second half, where John's disciples bring a complaint in verse 26, John answers, and the text slides into a reflection that is hard to attribute to anyone. The pattern is that every human voice grows smaller and the voice from above grows larger, which is exactly the Baptist's closing line, 'He must increase; I must decrease.'

The dialogue works through misunderstanding, a device John uses often. Jesus says something with two meanings, the hearer picks the lower one, and Jesus explains the higher. Here the pivots are the Greek word that can mean 'again' or 'from above,' and the word that can mean 'wind' or 'Spirit.' The humour is gentle. A learned man hears 'womb' where Jesus said 'heaven,' and Jesus replies with a wind that can be heard but not mapped.

Look at the pronouns. In verse 7 Jesus tells Nicodemus, singular, not to be amazed, and then says 'you must be born again' with a plural 'you.' In verses 11 and 12 He says 'we speak' and 'you people do not accept our testimony,' again plural. Nicodemus has come as the voice of a group, 'we know' in verse 2, and Jesus answers the whole group in his person. The passage also contains a steady stream of 'must' and 'cannot': no one can see, no one can enter, the Son of Man must be lifted up. It is a text about what lies beyond human capacity and is therefore sheer gift.

The final section is arranged around the bridegroom image, and it echoes the first. The one 'from above' of verse 31 recalls the 'from above' of verse 3 using the same Greek adverb. The 'testimony' that is not accepted, verse 11, returns in verse 32. The chapter is thus held together by an inclusion of birth from above and the One who comes from above.
context.historical:
Nicodemus is described as a Pharisee and a 'leader of the Jews,' which in John's usage means a member of the ruling council in Jerusalem. He reappears twice: in John 7:50-52 he asks that Jesus be given a hearing under the law, and in John 19:39 he brings a very large quantity of spices for the burial. The two later scenes show that the night visit was the start of a slow turning, not an instant conversion.

The Pharisees were the party most devoted to the Scriptures and to holiness, and they believed in the resurrection and in angels and spirits, unlike the Sadducees. Nicodemus therefore comes with a good deal of right belief, which makes it all the more striking that he is told he cannot even see the kingdom without a new birth. He is not an ignorant man. His problem is not lack of religion but lack of a life that religion cannot supply.

The night setting has more than one explanation. It may be prudence, since a member of the council risked his standing by seeking out a popular teacher the leaders had already begun to oppose, John 2:18. It may be practical, since night was the usual time for study and unhurried talk. And John clearly intends the symbol: 'night' and 'darkness' in his Gospel mark the absence of light, a theme that comes to a head in verses 19 to 21. The same Gospel says 'it was night' when Judas went out, John 13:30.

The second half places Jesus and John baptizing at the same time. Verse 24 notes that John had not yet been put in prison, which tells readers that this overlap belongs to an early period that the other Gospels skip over. Aenon near Salim is not certainly identified, but the text gives the reason for the choice, 'the water was plentiful.' The dispute with 'a certain Jew over the issue of ceremonial washing' shows how contested purification was. John 4:2 adds that it was Jesus' disciples, not Jesus, who actually baptized. And the Baptist's picture of the bridegroom's friend reflects wedding custom, in which a close friend arranged the match and stood by to hear the groom's voice, then rejoiced at the sound.
context.canonical:
Jesus answers Nicodemus out of the Old Testament, which is why he calls him 'Israel's teacher' and expects him to understand. The promise of Ezekiel 36:25-27 pairs clean water with a new spirit: God will sprinkle clean water on His people, remove the heart of stone, put His Spirit within them and cause them to keep His statutes. Ezekiel 37 then shows the Spirit, who is also the wind and the breath, bringing a valley of dry bones to life. Jeremiah 31:33 speaks of a law written on hearts, and Joel 2:28 and Isaiah 44:3 of the Spirit poured out. When Jesus speaks of water and Spirit, a teacher of Israel should hear all of this.

The lifting up of the serpent comes from Numbers 21:4-9. Israel, bitten by snakes for their complaining, looked to a bronze snake that Moses set on a pole and lived. Later, Hezekiah destroyed that same bronze snake when people began to burn incense to it, 2 Kings 18:4, which is a reminder that the sign was never the saviour. John uses the verb 'lift up' three times for Christ, John 3:14, 8:28 and 12:32, and in the last the narrator explains that He said this to show the kind of death He would die, 12:33.

Verse 16 is the Bible's best known sentence about love, and it rests on earlier words. Genesis 22:2 speaks of Abraham's son, 'your only son Isaac, whom you love,' offered on a mountain, and Romans 8:32 says that God 'did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all.' The Old Testament also supplies the invitation: 'Turn to Me and be saved, all the ends of the earth,' Isaiah 45:22. The apostles then preach the new birth: Peter says God 'has given us new birth into a living hope,' 1 Peter 1:3, Titus 3:5 speaks of 'the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit,' and 1 John 4:9-10 says that God sent His one and only Son so that we might live through Him.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John wants readers to see that the line between the kingdom and the outside runs through the center of religious respectability. Nicodemus is the best the system could produce, and he has to hear that something must happen to him that he cannot arrange. The author is not mocking him; he is showing that even the sincere and learned have no entry except by the free gift of God. The word 'must' in verse 7 is spoken to a good man.

He also wants readers to know that the gift has a ground. The conversation does not leave the new birth hanging in the air, because verses 14 to 16 tie it to the lifting up of the Son and the love of the Father. The first hearers could not have missed the allusion to the serpent, and they would have known that the cross is the means by which the Spirit's work becomes available. The author means them to see that the life God gives rests on what the Son does.

Finally, John sets before the reader a decision. Verses 19 to 21 do not describe a tragic accident but the way in which people respond to the Light. The chapter ends with the Baptist's contentment and a stark pair of outcomes in verse 36, so that nobody finishes the chapter without a question: do I come into the light, or do I stay away for fear of being seen? The patient story of Nicodemus, who reappears in chapters 7 and 19, shows that coming can be slow and still be real.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes a night conversation with one man and a dispute among John's followers. It does not prescribe a formula for conversion or a timetable, and it does not tell us that every believer will be able to point to a moment, any more than it explains how the Spirit moves. Jesus Himself says the Spirit is like the wind: you see the effects but not the mechanism. To demand a particular experience is to misread the image.

What it does prescribe, in the sense of declaring what is true for all, is that entry into the kingdom requires a birth from above, that this birth is the Spirit's work, and that faith in the lifted-up Son is how a person receives the life. These statements are not limited to Nicodemus. The universal words 'everyone who believes' and 'whoever' in verses 15 to 18 show that the offer is not confined to one setting.

It would also be wrong to take Nicodemus' visit by night as a pattern for secret faith. The text does not commend the darkness. It sets the later Nicodemus, who steps forward publicly at the burial, beside the one who came secretly, and it commends coming into the light so that what has been done may be seen clearly.

debates.question: What does 'born of water and the Spirit' mean in verse 5?

views.label: Christian baptism and the Spirit
views.case: Many in the early church read water as baptism, with the Spirit as the one who gives the new life it signifies. The immediate context of John's baptizing in the following verses supports a baptismal setting, and Titus 3:5 speaks of washing and renewal together.

views.label: Ezekiel 36: cleansing and a new spirit
views.case: Jesus expects a teacher of Israel to understand, and the Old Testament pairs water and Spirit in Ezekiel 36:25-27. On this view the two words describe one renewal, with water pointing to cleansing and Spirit to the new heart, and Nicodemus is faulted for missing a promise in his own Scriptures.

views.label: Natural birth, then spiritual birth
views.case: Some hold that water refers to physical birth, in line with verse 6, 'flesh is born of flesh, but spirit is born of the Spirit.' The point would be that two births are needed, one of the body and one of the Spirit, as Nicodemus's question about a womb had implied.

debates.bearing: The Ezekiel reading best fits Jesus' rebuke in verse 10, and it does not exclude the baptismal one, since John's Gospel never separates the sign from the Spirit's work it points to. What is not in doubt is that new life is from God by the Spirit.

debates.question: Where do Jesus' words end and the narrator's comment begin?

views.label: Jesus speaks to verse 21 and the narrator takes over
views.case: Verses 16 to 21 keep the themes of light and darkness from the prologue and use the vocabulary of the narrator, such as 'one and only Son,' which John applies to Jesus in his own voice in John 1:14 and 1:18. This reading is reflected in most modern quotation marks, which close at verse 15 or 21.

views.label: Jesus speaks throughout
views.case: There is no break in the Greek, and an unmarked change of voice is unusual. The 'for' that opens verse 16 links it to verse 15, and the discourse has already moved from 'we' to the Son of Man in the third person, which is a feature of Jesus' own speech.

debates.bearing: The text of the Gospel is inspired either way, so the doctrine does not hang on the answer. The practical point is that verse 16 belongs to the same argument as the lifting up of the serpent, and should not be read as a detached slogan.

debates.question: What is the main point of the wind image in verse 8?

views.label: Emphasis on the Spirit's sovereign freedom
views.case: The wind blows where it wishes, and no human technique can make it blow. On this view the verse is an answer to Nicodemus' 'how,' and it closes off the idea that the new birth can be earned or manufactured.

views.label: Emphasis on the evidence of the Spirit's work
views.case: The wind is heard, and its sound is a real evidence even if its path is not mapped. So the verse also teaches that new birth has recognizable effects, which John's first letter describes as righteousness and love, 1 John 2:29 and 4:7.

debates.bearing: The two readings fit together. The Spirit is free and cannot be commanded, yet He does not work invisibly in the sense of leaving no trace.

study.originalLanguages:
The first double meaning is anothen in verses 3 and 7. It can be 'again,' and Nicodemus takes it so, asking about a second entry into the womb with the word deuteron. But the same adverb means 'from above' elsewhere in the Gospel, in 3:31 of the One who comes from above and in 19:11 of authority given from above. Jesus is not asking for a repeat of the first birth but a different birth. The English phrase 'born again' keeps one sense and loses the other, and the best translations carry both in the margin. The verb for 'born,' gennao, can also mean 'begotten,' which fits a birth whose source is a Father.

The second is pneuma, which means breath, wind and Spirit alike, as the Hebrew ruach does. Verse 8 plays on it, 'the wind blows where it wishes,' and the choice of the verb 'wish' in a sentence about wind makes the wind a picture of the Spirit's will. This also explains Nicodemus' difficulty: the question 'how can this be' asks for a mechanism, but a wind is known by its effects. Ezekiel 37 uses ruach in the same triple sense, wind, breath and Spirit, in the valley of dry bones.

Third, hypsoo, 'lift up,' in verse 14. It is used literally of raising the serpent on a pole, but in John it is always a double word, for the cross and for glory. John 12:32-33 says that being lifted up would draw all people to Him and adds that this signified the kind of death He was to die. The same verb gives the Gospel its irony, since the moment of apparent defeat is the moment of exaltation. In Isaiah 52:13 the servant is 'lifted up' and 'highly exalted' in the Greek Old Testament, using the same verb, and the whole Gospel may be hearing that.

Fourth, the phrase in verse 16, 'one and only,' monogenes. It describes someone who is the only one of his kind, from a root that points to being one of a kind rather than to being begotten in time. Luke uses it for a widow's only son, Luke 7:12, and Hebrews for Isaac, Hebrews 11:17, which is exactly the offering of Genesis 22. 'So loved' translates a Greek word meaning 'in this way,' so the verse points first to the manner of the love, namely that He gave, and only then to its size. The verb 'perish' is the opposite of 'have eternal life,' a life of the age to come, as in Daniel 12:2.

Finally, notice the tenses of verse 18. The believer 'is not condemned,' but the one who does not believe 'has already been condemned,' a perfect tense that speaks of a standing state, and in verse 36 the wrath of God 'remains,' using meno, the verb of abiding. Even judgment is something that remains where the Light is refused. Verse 36 also sets 'believes' against a word that more literally means 'disobeys,' so that faith and obedience are treated as two sides of one response.

typology.type: The serpent on the pole, Numbers 21:8-9
typology.fulfillment: Israelites bitten by snakes were healed by looking at a bronze snake that Moses raised on a pole. Jesus says the Son of Man must be lifted up in the same way, so that everyone who believes may have life. The correspondence is of form and of means: a lifted-up figure, a look of trust, life for the dying. The escalation is from physical healing to eternal life, and from one camp to everyone who believes. John 12:32-33 shows that the lifting is the cross. The image of a serpent is not allowed to carry too much, though Paul does say that Christ became a curse for us, Galatians 3:13, and that God made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, 2 Corinthians 5:21. The type falls short in that the bronze snake could not forgive or change anyone, and Hezekiah later had to destroy it, 2 Kings 18:4.

typology.type: Clean water and a new spirit, Ezekiel 36:25-27
typology.fulfillment: Ezekiel promised that God would sprinkle clean water on His people, give them a new heart and put His Spirit within them. Jesus' words about water and Spirit take up this promise and present the new birth as its fulfillment, with the difference that it comes to those who believe in Him and reaches beyond Israel. The apostles use the same pattern: Paul says that God saved us through the washing of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit, Titus 3:5. The type falls short in that the prophecy spoke of a renewed nation, whereas the Gospel opens the new birth to everyone who believes, John 3:16.

Old Testament prophets describe the LORD as the husband of His people, Isaiah 54:5 and Hosea 2:19-20. The Baptist calls Jesus the bridegroom and himself the friend who stands and listens and is overjoyed at the voice. The friend's joy is complete when the groom is heard. John's whole ministry has been to bring the bride to Him. Paul later calls the church a pure bride presented to Christ, 2 Corinthians 11:2, and Revelation completes the picture with the wedding supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:7-9. The type falls short in that the friend has no claim on the bride, so John's willingness to decrease is not modesty but accuracy.

typology.type: The only son given on the mountain, Genesis 22:2
typology.fulfillment: Abraham was told to offer his only son, whom he loved, and God provided a ram in place of Isaac. John 3:16 speaks of the Father's love and the giving of His only Son, and Romans 8:32 draws the contrast that God 'did not spare His own Son.' The correspondence is that a beloved only son is given up in love. The escalation is that Isaac was spared and replaced, while the Son is not spared, so that the substitute is Himself the one given. The link rests on the shared themes of love and giving, not on a direct quotation of Genesis.

study.christ:
The conversation leads to Christ by a series of claims about Him that grow steadily larger, and it is worth taking them in order.

First, He is the one who knows and testifies. 'We speak of what we know, and we testify to what we have seen,' verse 11. A teacher of Israel has heard that the knowledge Jesus brings is first-hand. Then He is the one from above: 'No one has ascended into heaven except the One who descended from heaven, the Son of Man,' verse 13. The Old Testament asked who had gone up to heaven and come down, Proverbs 30:4, and Deuteronomy 30:12 spoke of the word as near and not to be fetched from heaven. John's answer is that One has come down to bring the heavenly things.

Second, He is the Son who must be lifted up. The 'must' of verse 14 is the necessity of the Father's plan, and the lifting up is the cross, which is also the throne. The Son of Man of Daniel 7 receives a kingdom, and John says that the way to that kingdom runs through the pole. The bronze snake in the wilderness had the likeness of what had harmed Israel, and the New Testament says Christ took the curse on Himself, Galatians 3:13. In the Gospel's next chapters He is called the Savior of the world, John 4:42, and in chapter 12 the lifted-up Christ draws all people to Himself.

Third, He is the gift of the Father's love, 'one and only,' and so is no mere messenger. The Father did not send a servant to condemn but His Son to save, and this is why the passage says that to believe in the Son's name is to be saved and to reject Him is to stand condemned already. The verdict is bound up with His person. John 5:22 says the Father has given all judgment to the Son, and verse 35 here says the Father has put all things in His hands.

Fourth, He is the Light, and the one who baptizes with the Spirit, John 1:33. The Spirit who produces the new birth is given by Him, which is why verse 34 says that God gives the Spirit without limit to the one He has sent. Nicodemus asks how he can be born from above; the answer is not a technique but a person whom he is looking at.

Fifth, He is the bridegroom. The Baptist's words in verses 29 to 30 make Jesus the center of a wedding and John the friend, and so tie the chapter back to the wine of Cana and the bridal imagery of the prophets.

The ending of the chapter keeps the picture honest. Not every detail of the serpent story is a picture of Christ; the snakes, the camp and the poison are not coded, and the New Testament does not elaborate them. The text itself makes one correspondence, the lifting up, and its meaning is given by John's own comment about the death He would die.
study.god:
This chapter shows God as the one who gives. Verse 16 is built on a single verb, 'gave,' and verse 27 states the principle for human life, 'a man can receive only what is given him from heaven.' God does not first wait for the world to improve. He gives His Son at the highest cost to Himself, and He gives the Spirit without measure, verse 34. The doctrine is that salvation begins in God's own love and not in any human condition, which is why the new birth cannot be earned.

God is also Father, Son and Spirit in distinct yet united action. The Father loves and gives and sends, verse 16 and 35; the Son descends, is lifted up and speaks the words of God; the Spirit gives birth from above. Jesus says that the Father has put all things in the Son's hands, which shows love that is shared, so that the Father's affection for the Son is not a loss but the source of the Son's gifts. A Trinitarian reading of verse 34 sees all three: the One sent, the God who sends, and the Spirit given.

The chapter does not soften God's holiness. The Light exposes deeds, the verdict is real, and the wrath of God 'remains' on those who refuse the Son. God's love and God's judgment are not set against each other, because the verdict is made known by the coming of the Light. His purpose in sending the Son was to save, verse 17, and the condemnation is not an extra act but the result of turning away from the only rescue. This holds a tension that every reader feels: a God who loves the world and a God who judges it, held together in a single verse.

God is sovereign in the Spirit's work, since the wind blows where it wishes, and yet He is the one who invites everyone. The chapter does not resolve how these fit, and it does not need to. It teaches that no one will be turned away who comes to the Light, verse 21, and that no one can claim credit for coming, since the one who comes has done so 'accomplished in God.'

For worship, then, the chapter shapes us in three ways. We praise a God who gave before we asked. We receive the new life as a gift and not a wage. And we learn from John the Baptist the posture of the worshiper: joy in hearing the bridegroom's voice and gladness that He must increase.

crossReferences.note: The setting for the lifting up of verse 14. Bitten Israelites who looked at the bronze serpent lived. Jesus names the pattern so that the cross is seen as God's appointed place of looking and living, and so that faith is understood as turning to what God has raised up, not as achieving something.

Hezekiah broke the bronze serpent in pieces because the people had begun to burn incense to it. This warns that a sign of God's saving work can be turned into an idol, and it sharpens John's point that what saves is the one lifted up, not any object or ritual associated with Him.

The promise of clean water, a new heart and God's own Spirit within His people. This is the passage that a teacher of Israel should have in mind when Jesus speaks of water and Spirit, and it is the best explanation for his surprise at Nicodemus' ignorance.

The breath enters the dry bones and they live. The Hebrew word for breath, wind and Spirit is the same, which makes the pun of John 3:8 a natural one for a Jewish teacher, and presents new birth as resurrection from a state of death.

Who has gone up to heaven and come down? Agur's question has no human answer in the Old Testament. John 3:13 gives it: only the Son of Man, who descended from heaven, can speak of heavenly things, and so the question of the proverb is answered in a person.

God told Abraham to offer his only son, whom he loved. The words 'only son' and 'love' meet in John 3:16, and the contrast is that Isaac was spared by God's provision, whereas the Father gives His Son as the provision for others.

A call for the ends of the earth to turn and be saved. It matches the structure of John 3:14-16, in which life comes to those who look to the One God has provided, and it supports the 'world' of verse 16, which reaches beyond Israel.

Jesus says that when He is lifted up from the earth He will draw all people to Himself, and John adds that this showed the kind of death He was going to die. This is the Gospel's own explanation of the verb in 3:14, and it removes any doubt that the lifting up is the cross.

God saved us not because of righteous things we had done but by His mercy, through the washing of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit. Paul's wording picks up the water and Spirit of John 3 and the Ezekiel promise behind it, and states plainly that the new birth is God's work and not our own.

Peter blesses God who has given us new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ. The new birth is here tied to the resurrection, which shows that the apostles read Jesus' words to Nicodemus as being fulfilled in the Easter life that He gives.

Nicodemus comes again, this time bringing a great weight of spices to bury Jesus. The man who came by night and could not understand a new birth now publicly honours the lifted-up Christ, and shows that the Spirit's work had gone on in him through years of silence.

study.oneStory:
From Genesis 3 the human story is a story of a dying life. Adam was made from the ground and the Spirit's breath, and sin brought the withdrawal of that life: death came to all. The prophets knew the problem went deeper than behavior. Israel needed more than new instructions, because the heart itself was hard and the law written on stone could not change it. Ezekiel promised a new heart and a new Spirit, and Jeremiah a new covenant written within. Meanwhile the wilderness generation showed how stubborn the problem was, perishing under snakes after repeated complaint, and rescued only by looking to what God had provided.

This chapter answers that long need. Jesus tells a good man that entry into God's kingdom is not an achievement but a birth from above, and that the new life promised by the prophets is now available through the Son who will be lifted up. It answers the question of how the curse of death is undone: not by trying harder, but by receiving life from the One who came down. It also answers the question about the nations, because the love of verse 16 is for the world, a hint of the Abrahamic promise that all nations would be blessed, Genesis 12:3.

It sets up what follows. In the next chapter the water offered to a Samaritan woman is the same gift in another image, and in John 7:37-39 the Spirit is poured out like rivers of living water after Jesus is glorified. The lifting up reaches its fulfillment in the cross and the resurrection, and at Pentecost the Spirit comes on the disciples, Acts 2:1-4. Paul calls this a new creation, 2 Corinthians 5:17, and the whole letter to Titus rests on the washing of rebirth.

The story ends where the first chapters began, with a world made new. Revelation 21:5 says, 'Behold, I make all things new,' and the river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, Revelation 22:1. Those who were born from above here enter a world where no one needs to fear the light, since there will be no night and no curse, Revelation 22:3 and 22:5, and the man who once came secretly in the dark is finally at home in the day.

quiz.q: What does Jesus tell Nicodemus is necessary to see the kingdom of God?

options.text: To be born again, born from above by the Spirit.
options.note: Verses 3 to 8 make the new birth from above by the Spirit the requirement.

options.text: To keep the law more carefully than the Pharisees.
options.note: Jesus says even Israel's teacher must be born again; law-keeping cannot achieve it.

options.text: To be cleansed and renewed inwardly by God.
options.note: True to the meaning of new birth, but it stops short of naming the birth from above by the Spirit.

options.text: To understand heavenly things through careful study.
options.note: Nicodemus was a learned teacher, yet study did not suffice; the need is new birth, not more learning.

quiz.q: What does the lifting up of the Son of Man like the bronze serpent point to?

options.text: Christ lifted up on the cross, so that all who look to Him in faith have eternal life.
options.note: Verses 14 and 15 apply Numbers 21 to Christ crucified and the life given to believers.

options.text: Christ ascending into heaven at the end of His ministry.
options.note: The lifting up in John refers first to the cross, not chiefly the ascension.

options.text: Christ being exalted and glorified through His death.
options.note: True, since lifting up carries the sense of exaltation, but the primary reference is the cross where He is lifted up.

options.text: Christ raising a physical banner over Israel.
options.note: The image is the serpent on the pole fulfilled in the crucifixion, not a military banner.

quiz.q: According to John 3:16, why did God give His one and only Son?

options.text: Because He loved the world, so that everyone who believes should not perish but have eternal life.
options.note: Verse 16 grounds the gift of the Son in God's love and its aim in eternal life for believers.

options.text: To condemn a sinful world for its rebellion.
options.note: Verse 17 says the opposite; God sent the Son to save the world, not to condemn it.

options.text: So that those who believe in Him would have eternal life.
options.note: True and central, but it leaves out that the gift flows from God's love for the world.

options.text: To reward those who already loved Him.
options.note: The love is God's initiative toward a world in darkness, not a reward for prior human love.

quiz.q: What is the verdict Jesus describes in verses 19 to 21?

options.text: The Light has come, but people loved the darkness because their deeds were evil.
options.note: Verse 19 defines the verdict as the response to the Light that has come.

options.text: God has already destroyed everyone who sins.
options.note: The verdict is about response to the Light; Jesus came to save, not to destroy at once.

options.text: People are judged by whether they come to the Light or hide from it.
options.note: A fair summary, but it omits the reason given, that people loved darkness because their deeds were evil.

options.text: Everyone will be judged only at the last day.
options.note: There is a final judgment, but here the verdict is already being rendered in how people respond to the Light now.

quiz.q: How does John the Baptist respond when told everyone is going to Jesus?

options.text: With joy, saying He must increase and I must decrease, for the bride belongs to the bridegroom.
options.note: Verses 29 and 30 show John's glad self-effacement before Christ.

options.text: With jealousy that his own following is shrinking.
options.note: The opposite; John rejoices to hear the bridegroom's voice.

options.text: By reminding them he is only the friend of the bridegroom, not the Christ.
options.note: True to his words, but it misses the joyful heart of his response, that Christ must increase.

options.text: By quietly withdrawing without explanation.
options.note: John does step back, but he explains his joy clearly rather than withdrawing in silence.

quiz.q: What does the chapter say is true of the one who rejects the Son?

options.text: He will not see life; the wrath of God remains on him.
options.note: Verse 36 states this plainly alongside the promise of life to those who believe.

options.text: He is given more time and no consequences follow.
options.note: Verse 36 says the wrath of God remains on him; rejection has grave consequences.

options.text: He remains under judgment until he believes.
options.note: True in substance, but softer than the text, which says the wrath of God remains on him.

options.text: He simply misses out on some extra blessings.
options.note: It is not a minor loss; verse 36 speaks of not seeing life and remaining under wrath.

questions: Jesus told a religious, moral, learned man that he still needed to be born again. Where are you tempted to trust your own goodness or knowledge instead of the new birth only God can give?
The new birth is like the wind, God's free and sovereign work. How does it comfort you, or unsettle you, that you cannot manufacture spiritual life but must receive it?
As the bitten Israelites looked to the serpent and lived, we look to Christ lifted up. What does it mean for you to simply look to Him in faith rather than trying to fix yourself first?
God so loved the world that He gave His Son. How does the costliness of that gift reshape the way you think about God's love for you?
John the Baptist said He must increase, I must decrease. In what part of your life is God calling you to step back so that Christ can be seen more clearly?

translationNotes.note: Born again renders anothen; the BSB footnote gives or born from above, also in verse 7. The word holds both senses, and Nicodemus's confusion turns on hearing only again.
The wind blows and everyone born of the Spirit uses one Greek word, pneuma, for both wind and Spirit; the wordplay pictures the sovereign, unseen work of the Spirit.
The BSB footnote notes that some manuscripts (BYZ and TR) add who is in heaven at the end of the verse; the sense of the Son of Man's heavenly origin is unchanged.
One and only renders monogenes; the BSB footnote gives or only begotten or unique, also in verse 18. The emphasis is on the Son's unique relation to the Father.
